# Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization

Younghyun Kim  , Wooseok Seo, Minseo Kim, Seunghyuk Oh, Minjae Lee  
Donghoon Kim, Hyung Il Koo, Jaehyung Kim, Wonjun Kang  
FuriosaAI Yonsei University University of California, Berkeley  Project
page:
[furiosa-air.github.io/elicitation-or-expansion](https://furiosa-air.github.io/elicitation-or-expansion)
 Code:
[github.com/furiosa-ai/elicitation-or-expansion](https://github.com/furiosa-ai/elicitation-or-expansion)

 Dataset:
[datasets/furiosa-ai/elicitation-or-expansion-trajectories](https://huggingface.co/datasets/furiosa-ai/elicitation-or-expansion-trajectories)
^(†)^(†)thanks: Equal contribution.  $`^{\dagger}`$Co-corresponding
authors.

###### Abstract

Recent studies in harness optimization have shown substantial
performance gains in language model agents without updating model
weights. A well-designed harness more effectively leverages the
underlying model’s capabilities by shaping context, tool use, and
execution workflows. However, naïve success rates alone do not fully
characterize whether optimized harness yields more reliable success on
tasks already within reach (_elicitation_) or a broader range of
solvable tasks (_expansion_). This distinction is crucial for recursive
self-improvement and evolutionary search, as expansion may provide a
broader range of successful experiences to push the capability
boundaries. Despite the growing significance, this distinction remains
underexplored in harness optimization. We conduct a systematic analysis
to study the effect of gains from harness optimization. Building on
$`\mathrm{pass@}k`$ analyses in the reinforcement learning (RL)
literature that compare models before and after RL training, we compare
optimized harnesses with their pre-optimization counterparts.
Specifically, we assess changes in reachable task coverage, compare
harness optimization with model scaling and increased inference-time
compute, and examine how gains vary with task difficulty. Across static
prediction and dynamic tasks, we find that $`\mathrm{pass@}1`$
advantages of harness over stronger interventions can reverse at larger
attempt budgets and aggregate gains conceal shortfalls on hard tasks,
underscoring the need for a fine-grained diagnosis.

## 1 Introduction

The ability of a language model agent is influenced by the design of its
_harness_, which governs prompting, context management, tool use, and
execution logic ([Young, 2025](#bib.bib31); [OpenAI, 2026](#bib.bib18)).
Refining these components can substantially improve agent performance
without updating model parameters, motivating growing interest in
harness optimization. By broadening the scope of harness optimization
beyond prompts ([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) and context ([Zhang
et al., 2026d](#bib.bib40)) to agent code and execution workflows ([Hu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib11); [Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib13)), recent
methods have achieved huge performance gains across diverse tasks.
However, these aggregate benchmark gains alone do not reveal which
aspects of the agent system have improved. For instance, comparable
gains arise either from simply reformatting otherwise correct answers to
satisfy the evaluation protocol or from enabling the agent to more
effectively leverage its environment and external feedback to deal with
previously unsolved tasks. This distinction is especially important for
approaches that leverage successful experience for subsequent
improvement, including recursive self-improvement  ([Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib38); [Lee et al., 2026a](#bib.bib12)). In these settings,
even rare successes on previously unreachable tasks can provide a
foundation for further search or learning.

Recent studies have begun to examine the nature of harness gains by
relating prompt edits to task-dependent performance changes ([Gong &
Wen, 2026](#bib.bib9)), attributing improvements to recoverable
execution defects ([Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)), and comparing
harness evolution with simple retries ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)).
However, these analyses leave open how task coverage under the original
and optimized harnesses differs as the attempt budget increases. Whether
the task coverage of optimized harness persists, disappears, or reverses
matters for assessing how far the optimized harness can extend an
agent’s practical problem-solving reach without further model training.
A closely related debate in reinforcement learning (RL) provides a
useful diagnostic perspective. Comparisons between RL-trained models and
their pre-RL counterparts show that improvements in $`\mathrm{pass@}1`$
can diminish or reverse at larger sampling budgets, suggesting improved
sampling efficiency rather than broader task coverage ([Yue et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33)). Other studies report broader coverage under the
valid reasoning evaluation ([Wen et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)) or
additional tool use ([Zhai et al., 2026](#bib.bib36)), while controlled
experiments show that coverage gains depend on pre-training exposure and
training-task difficulty ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib37)). Together,
these studies lay the ground for examining how improvements behave
across sampling budgets and task conditions, rather than inferring their
nature from a single aggregate score.

Figure 1: On HotpotQA, the optimized harness enables Qwen3-8B to

On easy questions, this advantage holds at both $`\mathrm{pass@}1`$ and

In this work, we investigate whether harness optimization makes success
more frequent on tasks already solved by the baseline (_elicitation_) or
broadens observed task coverage (_expansion_) through the lens of
$`\mathrm{pass@}k`$ ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib5)). We complement this
analysis by comparing optimized harnesses with base harness using larger
models from the same family or higher reasoning effort. These baselines
provide empirical reference for assessing how far harness optimization
alone enhances an agent’s capability. Finally, we examine whether gains
are concentrated on easier tasks or extend to harder ones.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization")
depicts why these multi-axis analyses matter. Here, overall
$`\mathrm{pass@}1`$ gain does not fully characterize harness gains; the
optimized harness leaves the agent less capable of solving harder
problems than under the original harness. Our analysis thus unveils
concealed coverage loss on harder tasks.¹¹ 1 This example uses an
optimized harness under relaxed per-attempt resource limits in
Appendix [C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Optimization Conditions ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization")

The heterogeneous effects recur throughout our analyses on various
benchmarks. First, advantages over stronger references can reverse as
the attempt budget increases: on LawBench ([Fei et al.,
2024](#bib.bib8)), the optimized GPT-OSS-20B harness exceeds the
GPT-OSS-120B baseline by $`16.05`$ percentage points (pp) at
$`\mathrm{pass@}1`$, but trails it by $`4.00`$ pp at
$`\mathrm{pass@}64`$. Second, on HotpotQA ([Yang et al.,
2018](#bib.bib28)) and AppWorld ([Trivedi et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)),
the selected harnesses approach or exceed stronger references in
aggregate but do not surpass them on hard subsets. Third, the
transferred text-classification harness falls below its baseline at
$`\mathrm{pass@}64`$ on all out-of-distribution datasets, despite small
$`\mathrm{pass@}1`$ gains on two. This heterogeneity makes systematic
analysis necessary: understanding harness gains requires distinguishing
reliability from coverage and examining how both change across attempt
budgets, task groups, reference systems.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Harness Optimization

Harness optimization adapts agent’s prompts, context, and execution
logic through repeated evaluation and revision. TextGrad ([Yuksekgonul
et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)) and GEPA ([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib2))
refine prompts through natural-language feedback, while ACE ([Zhang
et al., 2026d](#bib.bib40)) incorporates lessons from execution into an
evolving context playbook. Methods that search over agent code ([Hu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib11); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib38); [Zhang
et al., 2026e](#bib.bib41)) use execution feedback to diagnose failures
and guide revisions across harness components ([Lin et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib14); [Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib39); [Park et al.,
2026](#bib.bib19); [Yue et al., 2026](#bib.bib32)). Our study focuses on
Meta-Harness ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib13)), which uses a
coding-agent proposer to selectively inspects prior harness code,
evaluation scores, and execution traces for new candidates.

### 2.2 Interpreting Capability Gains

Analyses of reinforcement learning show that higher $`\mathrm{pass@}1`$
can accompany reduced coverage at large sampling budgets ([Yue et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33)), while other studies find broader coverage under
different training and evaluation conditions ([Wen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib24); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib37)). Recent work
further documents smaller gains on harder problems under standard
reinforcement learning and shows that adaptive sampling can improve
learning on these problems ([Noukhovitch et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)).
Studies of repeated sampling ([Brown et al., 2024](#bib.bib3)) and agent
interaction budgets ([Zhai et al., 2026](#bib.bib36)) examine how
additional attempts and interactions affect coverage, while test-time
scaling analyses show that effective compute allocation depends on task
difficulty ([Snell et al., 2025](#bib.bib21)). For harness optimization,
analyses compare evolution with test-time search ([Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)), trace gains to execution repairs ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib27)), and examine the repeatability ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib42)) and model dependence ([Lin et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib15)) of improvements. We analyze optimized harnesses
across attempt budgets and difficulty levels, distinguishing coverage
gains over the original baseline from advantages that persist against
baselines with larger models or more inference compute.

## 3 Analysis Setup

### 3.1 Preliminary: Harness Optimization

Let $`M`$ denote a solver model and $`H`$ its harness, which controls
model inputs, tool interactions, and execution state. On a task $`x`$,
executing $`(\mathcal{M},H)`$ yields a complete trajectory
$`\tau\sim\pi_{\mathcal{M},H}(\cdot\mid x)`$, evaluated by a
task-specific scoring function $`r(\tau,x)`$. Given a task distribution
$`\mathcal{X}`$, harness optimization seeks to maximize the expected
task score $`J(\mathcal{M},H)`$ by revising $`H`$ while keeping
$`\mathcal{M}`$ fixed:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\max_{H}\;J(\mathcal{M},H),\qquad J(\mathcal{M},H)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{X},\,\tau\sim\pi_{\mathcal{M},H}(\cdot\mid x)}\bigl[r(\tau,x)\bigr].
``` |  |

For our main experiments, we use Meta-Harness ([Lee et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib13)), whose coding agent, called proposer, selectively
inspects previous harness code, evaluation scores, and execution traces
to diagnose failures and propose revised harnesses. Each candidate is
evaluated, and its code and execution feedback are retained to guide
subsequent proposals. Our analysis compares the initial harness
$`H_{0}`$ with an optimized harness $`H^{\star}`$ selected based on
validation performance. We estimate their $`\mathrm{pass@}k`$ from
repeated executions on a common test set under the same task-specific
scorer
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Repeated Evaluation and pass⁢@⁢𝑘 ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization")).

### 3.2 Motivation: Beyond Mean Accuracy

Figure 2: Mean accuracy and coverage for harnesses from one optimization
run.

For a fixed set of tasks and number of attempts ($`k`$) per task,
$`\mathrm{pass@}1`$ determines the expected number of successful
executions (i.e., mean accuracy), whereas $`\mathrm{pass@}k`$ measures
the expected fraction of tasks solved at least once in $`k`$ complete
executions ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib5)) (i.e., coverage). A harness
can therefore achieve higher mean accuracy but low coverage, by
repeatedly solving the same tasks without obtaining successes on
additional ones. When generated solutions are used for
self-training ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib35)) or verifier-based
selection ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib6)), coverage is particularly
important as it captures the breadth of tasks for which a successful
example or solution is available.

Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Motivation: Beyond Mean Accuracy ‣ 3 Analysis Setup ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization")
compares $`\mathrm{pass@}1`$ and $`\mathrm{pass@}128`$ for Qwen3-8B
harness candidates from one optimization run, each evaluated on the same
300 HotpotQA tasks with $`k=128`$ executions per task. Although the two
metrics broadly track one another, the candidate with the highest
estimated $`\mathrm{pass@}1`$ differs from the one with the highest
observed $`\mathrm{pass@}128`$. Repeated evaluation can improve the
precision of $`\mathrm{pass@}1`$, but does not make it a substitute for
measuring task coverage at larger budgets.

## 4 Evaluation Setup

We refer to $`(\mathcal{M},H_{0})`$ and $`(\mathcal{M},H^{\star})`$ as
the baseline and optimized system, respectively. The reference
$`(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ref}},H_{0})`$ uses the base harness with a
larger solver model or the same solver model at higher reasoning effort.
We compare each system on a large $`k`$ attempts. More details are in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization").

### 4.1 Static Tasks

Text classification. Following [Lee et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib13), we
jointly optimize a single harness across three static prediction
datasets: Symptom2Disease ([Gretel AI, 2023](#bib.bib10)) for diagnosis
from symptom descriptions, LawBench ([Fei et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)) for
charge-set prediction, and USPTO ([Schneider et al., 2016](#bib.bib20))
for reactant-SMILES set prediction. In these tasks, the harness
constructs reference context to support prediction. We use a few-shot
harness as $`H_{0}`$, since directly supplying labeled examples provides
a simple way to construct such context. The optimized harness
$`H^{\star}`$ prepares memory from the same pool and retrieves relevant
information to construct context for each test input. Across
repetitions, $`H_{0}`$ resamples demonstrations and $`H^{\star}`$
rebuilds memory
(Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3 "Frozen memory. ‣ C.2 Static Tasks ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization")).
For out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer, we reuse $`H^{\star}`$ obtained
from in-distribution (ID) datasets to FiNER ([Loukas et al.,
2022](#bib.bib16)), GoEmotions ([Demszky et al., 2020](#bib.bib7)), and
Banking77 ([Casanueva et al., 2020](#bib.bib4)). We use
GPT-OSS-20B ([Agarwal et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) as $`\mathcal{M}`$ and
GPT-OSS-120B as $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ for comparison.

### 4.2 Dynamic Tasks

Multi-hop QA. On HotpotQA ([Yang et al., 2018](#bib.bib28)), the harness
coordinates evidence retrieval and answer generation. The base harness
$`H_{0}`$ follows multi-hop program of GEPA ([Agrawal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)): it retrieves passages, generates a follow-up query
from the retrieved evidence, and answers using summaries accumulated
across the two retrieval rounds. We obtain $`H^{\star}`$ by optimizing
the harness code governing query construction, evidence processing, and
answer generation, while keeping the BM25 retriever fixed. Evaluation
uses 300 test questions with their original difficulty labels. We use
Qwen3-8B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)) as $`\mathcal{M}`$ and
Qwen3-32B as $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ for comparison.

Agentic task. On AppWorld ([Trivedi et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)), the
harness coordinates multi-turn interactions with simulated applications,
where actions change the environment and execution feedback informs
subsequent decisions. The baseline harness $`H_{0}`$ follows the
benchmark’s simplified ReAct implementation ([Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib29)), alternating Python code generation and execution.
Evaluation uses the 168 tasks in test_normal with their original
difficulty labels. We use GPT-OSS-120B for both $`\mathcal{M}`$ and
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ref}}`$. The solver’s reasoning effort is fixed
at medium during harness optimization and for the base and optimized
systems; the reference system uses high reasoning effort.

## 6 Conclusion

We provide a diagnostic lens for understanding what harness optimization
improves, where its gains persist, and where performance shortfalls
remain. By combining $`\mathrm{pass@}k`$ curves with stronger reference
systems and analyses across task difficulty, we distinguish more
reliable success from broader observed task coverage. These diagnostics
help assess whether a harness suits an intended attempt budget and task
group.

Limitations and future work. Achieving consistent capability expansion
on hard tasks remains an important open challenge for harness
optimization, especially when successful executions support recursive
self-improvement or evolutionary search. This motivates search and
selection methods that reward validated successes on previously
uncovered hard tasks and retain candidates with complementary successes.
Large-budget $`\mathrm{pass@}k`$ analysis provides a diagnostic basis.
Our experimental results are bounded by the evaluated benchmarks, solver
families, and optimization runs examined in this study.

## Appendix A Repeated Evaluation and $`\mathrm{pass@}k`$

We repeat complete executions of each fixed solver–harness pair on the
same $`N`$ test tasks, including all internal model calls and tool
interactions. Let $`n`$ be the number of rollouts and $`c_{i}`$ be the
number of successes of task $`x_{i}`$. We estimate coverage within $`k`$
attempts following [Chen et al. (2021)](#bib.bib5):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{\mathrm{pass@}k}(M,H)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[1-\frac{\binom{n-c_{i}}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right],\qquad 1\leq k\leq n,
``` |  | (1) |

where the numerator is zero when $`n-c_{i}<k`$. Tasks are weighted
equally within each dataset or benchmark; text macro averages weight
datasets equally. At $`k=1`$, this is mean task success; at $`k=n`$ for
equal-sized pools, it is the fraction solved at least once.
Equation [1](#A1.E1 "In Appendix A Repeated Evaluation and pass⁢@⁢𝑘 ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization")
is unbiased under independent, identically distributed attempts from a
fixed policy.

## Appendix B Experimental Details

### B.1 Datasets and Splits

We follow prior split protocols, with sample sizes and adaptations in
Table [1](#A2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ B.1 Datasets and Splits ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization").
Symptom2Disease, LawBench, USPTO, and FiNER use the MCE splits ([Ye
et al., 2026](#bib.bib30)) distributed with Meta-Harness ([Lee et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib13)); GoEmotions ([Demszky et al., 2020](#bib.bib7)) and
Banking77 ([Casanueva et al., 2020](#bib.bib4)) derive from their public
releases. We subsample only examples with one annotated label from
official splits for GoEmotions to ease the evaluation. HotpotQA follows
GEPA’s split sizes ([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) using disjoint
subsets of the official fullwiki training set. AppWorld retains the
official train, development, and test_normal partitions ([Trivedi
et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)). Both dynamic benchmarks retain their
original difficulty labels.

| Dataset              | Prep. | Search/val. | Select. | Test |
|----------------------|-------|-------------|---------|------|
| Symptom2Disease (ID) | 200   | 50          | reused  | 212  |
| LawBench (ID)        | 200   | 50          | reused  | 100  |
| USPTO (ID)           | 50    | 30          | reused  | 100  |
| FiNER (OOD)          | 200   | —           | —       | 100  |
| GoEmotions (OOD)     | 200   | —           | —       | 150  |
| Banking77 (OOD)      | 200   | —           | —       | 150  |
| HotpotQA             | 150   | 300         | 300     | 300  |
| AppWorld             | 30    | 60          | 57      | 168  |

Table 1: Dataset sizes and split roles. Prep. supplies examples or tasks
to the harness; search/validation supplies optimization feedback. Reused
selection shares the validation set.

### B.2 Baselines and Harness Optimization

We use Meta-Harness ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib13)) with Claude Opus 5
as the coding-agent proposer, keeping solver weights fixed. Each
optimization allows 20 iterations with up to two proposals per
iteration.

#### Text classification.

We use GPT-OSS-20B for the baseline and optimized harness, with
GPT-OSS-120B as the stronger reference; all use medium reasoning effort
and temperature 0. Both baselines adapt the few-shot harness of [Lee
et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib13), resampling demonstrations for each query
and repetition within a pre-defined character budget. We select by
equal-dataset mean validation accuracy. The selected harness rebuilds
memory from preparation examples for each repetition. OOD evaluation
uses GPT-OSS-20B with the same preparation policy on target-domain
examples, without further code optimization.

#### HotpotQA.

We use Qwen3-8B with Qwen3-32B as the stronger reference, both at
temperature 0.6. The baseline follows GEPA’s multihop seed
program ([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) with BM25 retrieval. The
optimized harnesses are capped at four solver calls, two retrievals, and
seven passages per retrieval as well as the baseline. We shortlist
candidates using validation performance and select by exact match (EM)
on a separate selection set.

#### AppWorld.

We use GPT-OSS-120B at medium reasoning effort, with a high-effort
baseline as the stronger reference. Repeated evaluation uses
temperature 1. The baseline ports AppWorld’s simplified ReAct
agent ([Trivedi et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)). Each attempt permits 50
solver calls and 50 environment steps, with a 2,400-second timeout
extended to 7,200 seconds for high effort. Search and selection use
temperature zero and original TGC, with final selection on the
development set.

### B.3 Success Scorers

We apply the same scorer to all systems within each benchmark, relaxing
format requirements where necessary to better distinguish task
completion from format compliance. In text classification, we use binary
correctness after dataset-specific surface normalization. In HotpotQA,
to accept correct answers embedded in longer responses, we use
$`\mathrm{Judge}=(\mathrm{Contain}\land\mathrm{CORRECT})`$: answer
containment with an LLM judgment confirming correctness.
Table [2](#A2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ B.3 Success Scorers ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization")
gives examples that illustrate the failure mode from the Qwen3-32B
baseline in
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Do Optimized Harness Gains Differ by Task Difficulty? ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization").
Each complete response states the reference answer but receives EM = 0.
With 128 attempts per task, EM gives the Qwen3-32B lower
$`\mathrm{pass@}1`$ than Qwen3-8B, which is counterintuitive, whereas
Judge reverses this ordering. In AppWorld, we use arity-fixed TGC:
original successes remain successful, and an action attempt is
additionally accepted only if all state checks pass, no execution error
is recorded, and its sole failed check concerns an unrequested answer.
With 128 attempts per task, original TGC ranks the GPT-OSS-120B below
GPT-OSS-20B at $`\mathrm{pass@}1`$; arity-fixed TGC reverses this
ordering.

|  Question |  Reference answer |  Complete recorded answer |
|----|----|----|
|  Which band was formed first, Loudspeakers or Marcy Playground? |  Marcy Playground |  Marcy Playground was formed first. |
|  Which dog is larger, the Cirneco dell’Etna or the Siberian Husky? |  Siberian Husky |  The Siberian Husky is larger than the Cirneco dell’Etna. |
|  John Alexander is the uncle of the player who plays what position for Liverpool? |  right-back |  The player is a right-back for Liverpool. |
|  Intimidad de los parques was based on a short story by the novelist and essayist of what nationality? |  Argentine |  The novelist and essayist was Argentine. |
|  When was the direct-to-video movie that borrows heavily from a 1988 American action film starring Bruce Willis released? |  1996 |  The direct-to-video movie was released in 1996. |

## Appendix C Additional Experimental Results

### C.1 Variation Across Optimization Runs

We repeat harness optimization three times per benchmark and evaluate
the selected harness from each run.
Figure [12](#A3.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ C.1 Variation Across Optimization Runs ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization")
shows the mean and sample standard deviation (SD) across runs.
Evaluation uses 64 attempts per task for text classification and 128 for
HotpotQA and AppWorld. Mean gains over the original baseline shrink from
$`\mathrm{pass@}1`$ to the largest evaluated budget in all three
benchmarks. The amount of the gain varies across runs, but improved
single-attempt success does not consistently yield an advantage over
stronger references at larger budgets. In text classification, all three
optimized systems fall below the larger-model reference at
$`\mathrm{pass@}64`$. On hard HotpotQA and AppWorld tasks, none exceeds
the larger-model or higher-effort reference, respectively, anywhere
along the evaluated curves. SD includes evaluation and preparation; it
does not isolate optimizer variance.

### C.2 Static Tasks

#### Additional results on GPT-OSS-120B.

Single-attempt gains also do not improve $`\mathrm{pass@}64`$ for
GPT-OSS-120B. In
Figure [13](#A3.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ Additional results on GPT-OSS-120B. ‣ C.2 Static Tasks ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization"),
LawBench $`\mathrm{pass@}1`$ increases from $`27.95\%`$ to $`38.66\%`$,
while $`\mathrm{pass@}64`$ decreases from $`60\%`$ to $`59\%`$. The
optimized harness also has lower $`\mathrm{pass@}64`$ on
Symptom2Disease, and its USPTO curve remains below the baseline
throughout.

### C.4 Optimization Conditions

Relaxed resource limits do not yield higher mean coverage at $`k=128`$
in these runs. We compare three Qwen3-8B optimization runs per setting,
with caps of 4 solver calls, 2 retrievals, and 7 passages per retrieval
(tight) versus 12/12/20 (relaxed). Each run proposes 40 candidates on
the same optimization splits; the caps apply during both optimization
and evaluation.
````
